boot: Generating an issuer key pair and signing a demo credential…
cred.title: The credential
cred.note: A fictional driving licence from id.arcadia.example. Two separate decisions shape what a verifier ends up seeing: the issuer decides which claims may be withheld, and then the holder decides which of those to actually show. Change either column and the QR code rebuilds.
wire.title: What actually travels
qr.title: Presented code
verifier.title: Verifier
verifier.note: The result below is produced by verify() running against a pinned trust list and a cached status list. No request leaves the page.
attacks.title: Try to break it
attacks.note: Each button takes the credential above and does something an attacker would actually do, in plain string operations. The expected rejection code is printed on the button, so you can check the library against its own claims.
paste.title: Verify any payload
paste.note: Paste a QC1: envelope, or the raw SD-JWT form. Only the demo issuer is on this page's trust list, so a credential from anywhere else is rejected as an unknown issuer, which is the correct answer.
paste.label: Credential payload to verify
foot.tech: SD-JWT selective disclosure, base45 envelope, Token Status List revocation
tagline: Scan a credential and get an answer with no network connection. Everything on this page runs in your browser.
run.qrFail: QR renderer did not load. The payload below is still the real thing.
run.tooLarge: This payload is too large for any QR code. Make fewer claims disclosable.
run.passWhy: Signature checks out against a pinned issuer key.
run.failFacts: Nothing is trusted from a credential that fails, including its claims.
attack.0.label: Flip a claim in the payload
attack.0.note: Rewrites over_18 to true and leaves the original signature in place.
attack.1.label: Invent a claim that was never issued
attack.1.note: Appends a well formed disclosure the issuer never signed a digest for. Shown against a static presentation, because with a holder proof attached the sd_hash catches the tampering first and this check never gets a turn.
attack.2.label: Send the same disclosure twice
attack.2.note: A repeated disclosure is a cheap way to probe a sloppy verifier. Also shown against a static presentation, for the same reason.
attack.3.label: Sign it with the wrong key
attack.3.note: Same issuer name, same claims, a key that is not the pinned one.
attack.4.label: Claim to be another authority
attack.4.note: A perfectly valid credential from an issuer nobody pinned.
attack.5.label: Use it ten years from now
attack.5.note: The same honest credential, checked against a clock past its expiry.
attack.6.label: Use it after it was revoked
attack.6.note: Signature still perfect. The issuer set this credential's bit.
attack.7.label: Hide behind a stale status list
attack.7.note: An attacker who blocks updates cannot turn a maybe into a yes.
attack.8.label: Replay a recorded presentation
attack.8.note: The same scan, recorded and shown again later. The challenge has moved on.
attack.9.label: Present a photograph of this code
attack.9.note: A picture carries the issuer signature but cannot sign this scan. That is the whole point.
